form.2. SHORT COURSE DESCRIPTION: This course examines modern AI-native software development, where developers collaborate with increasingly capable coding agents. It covers how to define intent, provide effective context, structure development workflows, and coordinate AI tools. Students gain practical experience designing and evaluating agent-assisted software development processes.
form.3. TOPICS / CONTENT AREAS:
Treatment of this list: starting hypotheses — may add/drop/reorder with justification
A. AI-Native Development: AI-assisted coding, coding agents, developer workflows

B. Agentic Software Engineering: MCP, agent skills, tool use, context engineering

C. Specification & Planning: spec-driven development, requirements to executable specifications

D. Software Development Workflows: loop engineering, iterative development, software factories

E. Engineering Practice: automated testing, evaluation, deployment, reliability

F. Practical Development: hands-on coding, projects, emerging developer tools
form.4. COURSE INTENT:
Central question the course answers: How can software developers effectively
design and operate development workflows in which humans and AI agents
collaboratively build reliable software?

Pedagogical emphasis: Practical, workflow-oriented understanding through
hands-on development and experimentation.

This course should NOT become:
- A general introduction to AI or machine learning
- A traditional programming course
- A purely theoretical treatment of large language models

familiarity with advanced programming and basic software engineering concepts.

project-based evaluation, and a final project.

existence.reason: While CSE701 covers AI in Software Engineering focusing on data mining, defect prediction, and ML applications in software engineering, the new course focuses on modern AI-native software development, coding agents, agentic workflows, and human-AI collaborative development practices.
existence.recommendation: Proceed as a distinct course. It complements CSE701 by focusing on interactive agentic workflows and AI-assisted development tools rather than historical data mining and predictive models.

overlaps.differentiation: CSE701 investigates mining software repositories and applying machine learning models to software engineering artifacts, whereas this course emphasizes practical, workflow-oriented design of agentic software development and coding agents.

CSE594A focuses primarily on agentic reasoning for algorithmic and mathematical problem solving, whereas this course targets software engineering workflows, coding agents, and spec-driven software development.
CSE582 covers traditional software evolution, product lines, and maintenance, whereas this course deals with AI-native development and software factories driven by coding agents.
CSE581 deals with classical systems analysis, design theories, and requirements engineering, whereas this course covers automated requirements and spec-driven development using AI.
AI501 provides foundational machine learning theory and models, whereas this course uses AI tools in applied software development workflows.
CSE201 teaches object-oriented programming and manual unit testing in Java, whereas this course focuses on automated testing and evaluation in AI-assisted developer workflows.
CSE665 covers large language model architectures and NLP principles theoretically, whereas this course focuses on practical software engineering workflows with coding agents.
CSE583 covers open source tools and development methods, whereas this course focuses on AI-native agentic development.

prerequisites.justification: Students need solid software engineering fundamentals, unit testing, and advanced programming capabilities to evaluate and work with AI-generated code.
Familiarity with machine learning evaluation metrics helps students understand the reliability and evaluation of AI coding tools.

narrative.course_description: This course examines modern AI-native software development, where developers collaborate with coding agents. It covers how to define intent, provide effective context, structure development workflows, and coordinate AI tools. Students gain practical experience designing and evaluating agent-assisted software development processes. The curriculum addresses AI-assisted coding environments, agent skills, model context protocols, requirements engineering with executable specifications, automated testing, and software factory architectures. The course is taught through lectures, tutorials, and laboratory sessions emphasizing hands-on development and experimentation. Upon completion, students will be able to construct developer workflows incorporating AI-assisted coding tools, implement agent skills and context engineering mechanisms, translate informal requirements into executable specifications, evaluate reliability and performance of AI-generated code, and architect end-to-end agentic software development factories.
narrative.sequencing_rationale: The modules progress from foundational AI-assisted coding workflows (M1) to advanced agent skills and context engineering (M2), followed by requirements and executable specifications (M3), automated testing and reliability evaluation (M4), and finally integrated agentic software factories and deployment (M5). This sequence relies on foundational programming skills from CSE201 and gradually builds toward complex multi-agent architectures.
narrative.assessment_rationale: The assessment scheme combines quizzes (10%), assignments (20%), a project (25%), midsem (20%), and endsem (25%). This mix balances theoretical comprehension with practical competencies such as implementing agent skills, evaluating reliability, and executing live scenarios as specified by the course outcomes.
narrative.positioning_rationale: While CSE701 investigates repository mining and machine learning models for software engineering, and CSE594A focuses on agentic reasoning for mathematical problems, this course targets practical workflow-oriented design of agentic software development and coding agents. Other courses such as CSE582, CSE581, AI501, CSE201, CSE665, and CSE583 address traditional evolution, classical systems analysis, machine learning theory, manual unit testing, or open-source tools rather than AI-native agentic software factories.
